newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BT clouds MCI terms as profits rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BT clouds MCI terms as profits rise.

text.p: British Telecommunications' proposed $20 billion merger with America's MCI raised fresh analyst concerns on Thursday after the British telephone giant said parts of the merger agreement had not been published.

Despite a surprise profit warning from MCI three weeks ago, some analysts say it is increasingly likely the deal will go ahead on unchanged terms -- possibly towards the end of next month -- to avoid legal action by MCI.
"I think they are going to go forward with the deal without renegotiating it because they are worried about MCI's lawyers," said one analyst, who declined to be named.

After reporting a modest 1.4 percent rise in first quarter pre-tax profits to 881 million pounds ($1.4 billion), BT sparked fresh worries that it might have unwittingly signed a deal which ruled out renegotiation because of difficulties in the local U.S. phone market.
Although BT said it supported MCI and its local investment plans, BT told analysts that it was not only investigating MCI's local and core long-distance businesses but the whole merger agreement.
BT has always denied speculation that it has signed a separate side letter to the main merger agreement which does not allow it to push for fresh terms.

But analysts wonder whether the parts of the deal that have not been published because they contain confidential commercial information include details about MCI's costly plans to break further into lucrative U.S. local markets.
"If there is no secret agreement why try and cloud the issue more?" asked one analyst who declined to be named.
BT declined to comment on whether there was any part of the merger, published or unpublished, which disallows a fresh deal because of problems in MCI's local business.

A spokesman said only that the issue was complex and that simplistic information could be inaccurate. "We are dealing with very complex legal issues and the danger is that simplistic information could well be inaccurate," he said.

BT will also not comment on the progress of its crucial review of MCI, led by top BT and MCI executives. Finance director Robert Brace confirmed only that it was likely to take weeks rather than months.
BT shares lost 3.5p, falling to 427p by late afternoon trade despite higher-than-expected profits, because of uncertainty over the future of the merger.
MCI surprised and disappointed BT by forecasting losses of $800 million this year and more next year because of delays breaking into lucrative local U.S. telephone markets.

Analysts here described as "gung-ho" MCI's decision to throw money at the problem by stepping up investment despite what MCI called foot-dragging by monopolistic local U.S. operators and the slow pace of U.S. local telephone deregulation efforts.
But BT's finance director Robert Brace said BT backed the local investment plans of MCI, which on Wednesday reported a 6.7 percent drop in second quarter net income to $280 million.
"I think BT is very supportive of MCI and its attempts to develop business in the local (market) and in its calls for the regulators to open up markets," he told Reuters.

It remains unclear whether BT will demand that MCI reins in its local capital expenditure programme with which it hopes to offset increasingly competitive international and long-distance telephone prices.

As some institutional investors are growing increasingly irritated by a perceived news blackout ahead of the review's completion, Brace emphasised the complexity of analysing facts and determining the best way forward.
"It isn't a question of checking the books as such. It's a question of taking a view on what is likely to happen going forward," he said.

BT, which is looking abroad to help boost growth amid rising competition from cable companies at home, said start-up costs of European joint ventures ahead of European liberalisation next year and a lower contribution from MCI, helped keep a lid on profits.
But first quarter pre-tax profits were flattered by a lower-than-expected redundancy charge and a 20 million pound exceptional profit on sales. Group turnover rose 4.3 percent to 3.8 billion pounds.
Turnover from inland telephone calls was virtually static at 1.23 billion pounds and volume growth was offset almost entirely by over 200 million pounds of price cuts.
However, both inland and international call volume growth over a 12 month period rose to eight percent from around seven percent, BT said. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
